extracted.intended_audience: Machine learning researchers, program committees, conference and journal boards
extracted.subtask_short: Bengio's critique of the ML publication process and proposed reforms
extracted.subtask_description: Blog post by Yoshua Bengio arguing that the conference-driven ML publication process produces incremental, error-prone, half-baked work and proposes a slower, journal-first model. Each substantive critique or reform principle is treated as a rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and depth suffer from fast-paced productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: So we are more productive, on the surface, but this stress, productivity fast pace have a price on the depth and quality of the papers we produce. Many papers end up being submitted that in the past would not have been submitted. They may contain errors, lack in rigour or simply be rather incremental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bengio frames the field's rapid output cadence (a new conference deadline every ~two months) as a structural cause of lower-quality, error-prone, incremental work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadline rush prevents careful checking
rubrics_metrics.description: In the rush preceding a conference deadline, many papers are produced, but there is not enough time to check things properly and the race to put out more papers (especially as first or equal-first author) is humanly crushing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cadence imposes both a scientific cost (insufficient time to verify results) and a human cost (crushing pressure on students and researchers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Important advances require slow, deep thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: On the other hand, I am convinced that some of the most important advances have come through a slower process, with the time to think deeply, to step back, and to verify things carefully. Pressure has a negative effect on the quality of the science we generate. I would like us to think about Slow Science (check their manifesto!).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bengio explicitly endorses the Slow Science manifesto as an antidote: paper quality benefits from time to think, step back, and verify carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Current system incentivizes incremental work
rubrics_metrics.description: My feeling is that besides the poor incentives for reviewing, our current system incentivizes incremental work and creates a lot of pressure and stress on grad students (and researchers in general) to submit as many papers as possible at each deadline. Students sometimes come to me two months before a deadline asking if I have ideas of something which could be achieved in two months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: students framing research as 'what can I finish in two months' rather than pursuing deeper, longer-horizon work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission lottery wastes community resources
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition, we now have a bunch of ML conferences (in particular NeurIPS, ICML and ICLR) with a strong overlap in their content and community, so people just resubmit their rejected work to the next conference and draw a new sample of reviewers (and because of the noise, it means a paper eventually gets accepted, after using a lot of resources from the community).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The overlap between top ML conferences plus noisy reviewing creates a resubmission lottery where rejected papers eventually get accepted just by re-rolling the reviewer sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer shortage and bursty demand harm assignment quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Plus the fact that all good reviewers are in demand at very specific weeks of the year makes it harder for area chairs to find the appropriate reviewer for their paper (unlike what happens with journals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bengio contrasts the conference model's bursty reviewer demand with journals, where assignment is spread throughout the year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal-first model with conference selection from accepted pool
rubrics_metrics.description: This brings to mind a different model, one where papers are first submitted to a fast turnaround journal (which could be JMLR in this case) and program committees of each conference then pick the papers they like the most from the list of already accepted and reviewed (and scored) papers (assuming the authors are interested in having their work presented at a conference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed reform: decouple peer review (handled by a fast-turnaround journal such as JMLR) from conference selection (which curates from the pool of already-accepted papers). Similar to what has been experimented at venues like VLDB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conferences should highlight and synchronize, not gate publication
rubrics_metrics.description: In the old days, conferences were important to speed up the research cycle and have a fast turnaround of ideas. But now we have arXiv which plays that role much better, so the main role of conferences, besides the socializing, should be to select work to be highlighted and presented orally, to create a diversified offer of the best and most important ideas arising in our community, to synchronize researchers around this progress. It doesn't even have to be super-recent work, it could be work which got done 1 or 2 years ago and is only recently picking up steam in terms of impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conferences should serve as curatorial and social/synchronization venues, not as the primary archival gatekeepers; selected work need not be recent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadlines incentivize submitting half-baked work
rubrics_metrics.description: The deadline system of conferences creates an incentive to submit half-baked work (and often not even fix things properly later if the paper is accepted, rather move on to another publication). If there is an implicit soft deadline (because if I submit my paper now to JMLR there is uncertainty as to when it will be accepted and available for selection by a conference) then there is an incentive to continue working on the paper until it is better polished, rather than submit it too early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: authors move on to the next paper instead of fixing accepted-but-flawed work. Softer, uncertain deadlines (as in journal submission) reward continued polishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative journal feedback improves final quality
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition, the richer iterative feedback of the journal process should lead to higher-quality results at the end of the day. And having our work in journal form would make it easier for ML researchers to collaborate with researchers in other disciplines who value journals and not conferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal review's repeated revision cycles are framed as producing higher-quality final papers, with the side benefit of enabling cross-disciplinary collaboration with fields that privilege journals.
